title: Asking and Answering Your Own Questions
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece examines a specific rhetorical habit — posing a question and then immediately answering it oneself — as a subtle marker of confidence that can tip into arrogance when overused. It situates the habit within a broader set of confidence cues, including vivid language and direct eye contact, and warns that stacking too many such cues too quickly produces a "Titanic effect" where an audience starts to read conviction as hubris. The author encourages leaders to notice when they deploy this device, particularly in moments of high emotional charge, and to use it more sparingly and self-consciously.
points: Asking and immediately answering one's own question is a common but often unconscious cue leaders use to project confidence.
Overusing any single confidence marker can flip a leader's image from convicted to arrogant — the "Titanic effect."
The habit tends to surface most when leaders are highly charged or emotionally convicted about an issue.
Leaders are often unaware how frequently they rely on particular confidence markers in conversation.
Building self-awareness about these verbal habits helps leaders calibrate a more credible, less self-important style.
quotes: The best leaders are highly aware of the markers or cues of confidence that they use to project self-assurance.
Too many cues deployed too quickly can transform a confident leader into one viewed as arrogant or condescending.
One marker or cue worthy of examination is the device of asking and answering one’s own questions.
Overusing any marker of confidence produces a “Titanic effect” where others are more likely to view you as arrogant or full of hubris.
Becoming more aware and intentional about how you project confidence is critically important for developing a style that works best.
